q: Which component is the **only** one that reads from and writes to etcd directly?
options: kube-apiserver
kube-scheduler
kube-controller-manager
kubelet
explain: All other components go through the API server, which handles authentication, authorization, admission and validation before persisting to etcd. This hub-and-spoke design lets components be replaced independently.

q: You run `kubectl delete pod web-7d9f-abcde`. The pod belongs to a Deployment with `replicas: 3`. A new pod appears seconds later. Which component created the new Pod **object**?
options: The Deployment controller
The scheduler
The kubelet on the node that ran the old pod
The ReplicaSet controller
explain: The ReplicaSet controller counts pods matching its selector and creates Pod objects to reach the desired count. The Deployment controller manages ReplicaSets, not pods. The scheduler only assigns a node; the kubelet only runs pods already bound to its node.

q: New pods in your cluster stay `Pending`. `kubectl describe pod` shows `Node: <none>` and **no events at all**. What is the most likely cause?
options: Not enough CPU on any node
No scheduler is running (or none serves the pod's schedulerName)
The image cannot be pulled
The CNI plugin is broken
explain: A running scheduler that cannot place a pod records a `FailedScheduling` event (for example `Insufficient cpu`). Complete silence means nothing tried. Image pulls and CNI problems happen after binding, so the pod would have a node and kubelet events.

q: Which statements about the kube-scheduler are true? (select all)
options: It filters out nodes that cannot run the pod, then scores the rest
It starts the containers on the chosen node
It writes a Binding that sets the pod's `spec.nodeName`
It considers resource **requests**, taints/tolerations and affinity rules
explain: The scheduler's whole job is choosing a node and recording that choice via a Binding. The kubelet on that node then notices the pod and starts its containers through the CRI.

q: Your CI pipeline runs `kubectl apply -f k8s/` and immediately marks the deploy as successful. Why is this wrong?
options: `apply` returns once desired state is stored; pods may still be pulling, crashing or failing readiness
`apply` only works on single files
`apply` requires `--wait` to send anything to the server
`apply` is asynchronous only on managed clusters
explain: Kubernetes is eventually consistent. The API server responds after persisting the object; controllers, the scheduler and kubelets do the work afterwards. Gate pipelines on `kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> --timeout=...` or `kubectl wait`.

q: What does it mean that Kubernetes controllers are **level-triggered**?
options: They only react to events with a high priority level
They process events strictly in the order received and fail if one is missed
They act on the current observed state compared to desired state, so missing individual events does not matter
They run at fixed log levels
explain: A level-triggered controller looks at the world as it is now and converges, so a restart or a burst of changes is harmless. An edge-triggered design would depend on processing every event exactly once.

q: Which of these run on **every** worker node? (select all)
options: kubelet
etcd
A container runtime such as containerd
kube-proxy (unless replaced by a CNI like Cilium)
explain: Worker nodes need the kubelet to run pods, a CRI runtime to create containers, and usually kube-proxy for Service routing. etcd runs on control-plane nodes (or externally), never on ordinary workers.

q: On a kind cluster you delete the pod `kube-apiserver-kind-control-plane` from `kube-system`. What happens?
options: The API server stops and the cluster becomes unusable
The kubelet recreates the mirror pod; the real container keeps running because it is defined by a static manifest on disk
The ReplicaSet in kube-system recreates it
The scheduler moves the API server to a worker node
explain: Control-plane components on kubeadm/kind clusters are static pods defined in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`. The API object is only a mirror. To stop a static pod you remove its manifest file from the node.

q: A Deployment shows `metadata.generation: 7` and `status.observedGeneration: 6`. What does this tell you?
options: The Deployment has been rolled back once
There are 6 ready replicas out of 7
The object is corrupt in etcd
The controller has not yet processed the latest spec change
explain: `generation` increments on every spec change; the controller copies it to `status.observedGeneration` once it has acted on that spec. A lag means the change has not been reconciled yet (or the controller is down).

q: Which are good uses of **labels** (rather than annotations)? (select all)
options: `app.kubernetes.io/name: shipit-api` so a Service can select the pods
A 40 KB JSON blob of build metadata
`environment: staging` so you can `kubectl get pods -l environment=staging`
The git commit SHA and a link to the CI run, for humans to read
explain: Labels exist for identification and selection, and values are limited to 63 characters. Large or descriptive metadata that nothing selects on belongs in annotations (up to 256 KiB total).

Deployment
PersistentVolume
Service
explain: PersistentVolumes, Nodes, StorageClasses, Namespaces, ClusterRoles and CRDs are cluster-scoped. PersistentVolumeClaims, by contrast, are namespaced. Check with `kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false`.

q: "Kubernetes removed dockershim in v1.24." What does this mean for an image you build with `docker build` on your Mac?
options: Nothing: it is a standard OCI image and runs on containerd or CRI-O just the same
It must be rebuilt with buildah
It can only run on nodes that still have Docker Engine installed
It must be converted with `kind convert`
explain: Only the node's runtime integration changed: the kubelet now talks CRI to containerd or CRI-O instead of Docker Engine. Images are OCI-standard and portable. (Do watch out for CPU architecture: arm64 vs amd64.)

q: Which component creates a cloud load balancer when you create a `Service` of `type: LoadBalancer` on EKS or GKE?
options: kube-proxy
kube-scheduler
CoreDNS
cloud-controller-manager (or the provider's load balancer controller)
explain: Cloud-specific logic lives in the cloud-controller-manager (and on AWS often in the separate AWS Load Balancer Controller). kube-proxy only programs node-local rules for routing Service traffic.
